topic.title: Translating the Content Fusion user guide — lessons learned
topic.shortdesc: A journal of translating our own user guide: what an uninstructed run got wrong, the two workspace files that fixed most of it, and the two things they made worse.

body.p: Leveraging AI, Content Fusion can translate your documentation automatically. But even with AI, no translation can be right without context: your product's terminology, and the terms your team has settled on. What follows is a journal of translating our own user guide, and what we found when we reviewed the result.

section.title: Baseline translation
section.p: We wanted to translate our user guide into several languages, using the new Content Fusion translation feature, to dog-food our own tools.
We used four topics instead of the entire guide to keep the evaluation focused and efficient. The issues described below are systematic, so this smaller sample was sufficient to identify them.
As a baseline, we ran a translation job with no instructions, then reviewed the result with AI and with a native French speaker.

ol.li: The terms our app puts on screen came out translated differently — the AI had no way to know how our own UI is translated. The guide said validations entrantes where the product says Commits entrants, and called the role Réviseur where the label is Examinateur. Eight terms, around twenty occurrences. Two thirds of the labels happened to come out right, which is worse than it sounds: it makes the output look reviewed.

The text was mostly grammatically correct, but it did not read like something a native speaker would write. bande for a UI strip, where French wants bandeau; certains membres sélectionnés, a pleonasm; prendre en charge for a review task, which does not handle a workflow but is part of one.

The same English term came out differently in different files — dépôt six times in one topic, référentiel twice in the next, and never mixed inside a single file. Each file was consistent with itself and disagreed with its neighbour.

Bold moved. The English bolds only the role name; the French widened <b> over the whole phrase in two files and got it right in a third. Elsewhere the article was pulled inside, so the emphasized string was no longer the product term.
Real grammar errors, which we had not expected: a missing plural agreement in an <indexterm> (Tâches de révision indépendante) — correct in one file, wrong in its parallel one.
No French typography. French puts a non-breaking space before : ; ! ?; there was not a single one in the whole translation.

section.p: To address these, we involved 2 files: a glossary & agent instructions.

section.title: The glossary
section.p: Two files, both in .contentfusion/i18n/, both committed next to the documentation. Everything in them is there because a specific defect happened.
Our shipped French UI lives in a resource bundle in the application's repository, which the agent — sandboxed to the DITA workspace — cannot read. So the glossary goes in the workspace:
section.codeblock:
## Not translated by the product — shown in English - `DITA Map` (key `ditamap`) - `Org-level role` (key `organization.role`)
## Labels - `Incoming commits` -> `Commits entrants` - `Repository` -> `Dépôt` - `Add reviewer` -> `Ajouter un examinateur` - `Software Docs Starter` -> `Documentation logicielle - Guide de démarrage` ...
section.p: That first list earns its place as much as the pairs do. Where the running UI shows English for a label, the manual has to as well — 18 labels for French, 13 for German, only 8 of them in both — and you only know which by looking them up per language.

section.title: The instructions
section.p: .contentfusion/i18n/agent-instructions.md is read verbatim before the run and applies to every translation in the project, unlike the per-job Translation Instructions field. Here it is in full — this is the file that produced the results below.
section.codeblock: ### Terminology — the shipped UI is the authority .contentfusion/i18n/ui-glossary-fr-FR.md holds the product's shipped en→fr UI strings. Read it before translating. Any text inside `` or ``, and every button, field, view, page, and role name, must reuse the shipped French string verbatim. Never invent a French label that contradicts a shipped one. If a label is absent from the glossary, translate it once and reuse that exact rendering everywhere. One English term maps to exactly one French term for the entire run — across every file. Fix your rendering of these before you start and never vary it: repository, commit (noun vs. verb), workspace, workflow, and each platform and task role name. ### Inline markup fidelity Preserve the exact scope of every inline element. The words emphasized in the source must be the words emphasized in the target — never widen ``/`` to swallow an article, preposition, or the surrounding phrase, and never narrow it. `Author platform user role` → `rôle d'utilisateur de la plateforme Auteur`, not `rôle d'utilisateur … Auteur`. ### French typography Use a non-breaking space (U+00A0) before `:` `;` `!` `?` and inside `« »`. Never a plain space. ### Delegation Translate clusters of semantically related topics (e.g. chapters, sub-chapters) in a single "dita-translator" sub-agent.
section.p: Two lines in it are less reliable than they look. The typography rule worked on this run — but the agent produced 11 of the 12 spaces as the character entity   rather than the literal character the rule asks for, and on an earlier run it reported that it could not emit the character at all:
section.codeblock: I was unable to reliably insert a genuine non-breaking space (U+00A0) before `:` through the available editing tools in this session — several attempts to inject the character were silently normalized to a regular space by the tool layer. [...] I used a normal space before colons.
section.p: So ask for the entity yourself: it is plain ASCII and survives every layer between the model and the file. And the delegation rule is the weakest thing in the file — the agent's own translation skill specifies one worker per resource, and a project instruction does not clearly outrank a skill, so expect it to be applied inconsistently until the default changes.

section.title: Results after re-running
section.p: Same agent, same model, same four topics. The only change was those two files. Because runs are incremental we deleted the translated files first, so the diff is exactly the effect of the new context and nothing else.

Same term rendered differently per file

section.p: We ran German the same way, as sibling branches off one commit, and it moved the same way: two invented UI labels became zero, both having been in the glossary all along; a sentence duplicated across two topics that came back as der Merge in one and das Merge in the other settled on a single rendering at all four sites; and four German compounds the baseline had broken across a line break at the hyphen — the published page reading Git- Anmeldedaten, because XML collapses that newline to a space — came back intact.

And two things the instructions made worse. Our German glossary stated the quotation-mark rule correctly and then demonstrated it with an ASCII " as the closing character instead of „'s partner “. The agent followed the example rather than the sentence, and every quoted label in the German output shipped wrong — something the uninstructed baseline had got right on its own. A bad instruction is worse than no instruction, and it fails uniformly across every file, which makes it harder to catch in review rather than easier, because nothing looks locally inconsistent.

Second: our English source contains a ( that never closes. The baseline quietly repaired it; the instructed run, told to preserve the source structure faithfully, shipped the bug. Tightening the instructions costs you the model's free proofreading, so fix your source rather than relying on it.

section.title: A repeatable workflow for your documentation
section.p: None of this is specific to Content Fusion, or to French. The loop:

ol.li: Pick a small publication — a handful of topics — to develop against.
Run a job with no instructions. That is your baseline, and it may already be good enough for internal drafts.

Find out whether your product's UI is already localized: resource bundles, .properties files, i18n JSON, message definitions. If a target-language UI exists, it outranks the translator's judgement on every label.
Generate a per-locale glossary from that bundle, filtered to labels. Carry through the labels the product deliberately leaves in English as well.
Write the project instructions: terminology, frozen terms, typography, markup fidelity, delegation. Proofread your literal examples character by character.
Put both files in the workspace, where the agent can read them.
Review with AI first, then with a person; re-translate; diff. Feed what you find back into step 5.
Point it at the real publication, and commit the instructions and the glossary with the docs.

section.p: Copy the structure and not the text when you add a language. agent-instructions.md is a single fixed path that every target language reads, so name the language in each heading — ### French typography, not ### Typography. That is not cosmetic: French wants a non-breaking space before : and German wants none at all, so a rule you assumed was universal will corrupt the second language you add. Working from the same bundle, our own two locales agree on very little:
Not one of those rows is predictable from the other column. You look this up per language, or you get it wrong — which is exactly why the glossary step exists.

ol.li: Terminology is data, not inference. The AI can write fluent prose in the target language and still contradict every button in your product. The shipped UI strings are the authority, the agent cannot see them, and no instruction substitutes for putting them in the workspace.
Develop against a small sample. Four topics were enough to expose defects that are systematic by nature. Only the scale of each problem needs the real publication.

Encode rules in forms the tooling can preserve. The non-breaking space was requested, attempted, and on one run reported as impossible; a character entity survives. And a rule demonstrated with a malformed example loses to the example, uniformly, in every file.
Verify with AI and with a person. The AI review found the terminology, typography and markup problems quickly, across the whole tree, with file and line references.
